answer.rationale: The finance mandate is non-negotiable: an 18% cut to component spend this year. memory_c2 records that the low-cost vendor already delivered a sharp unit-cost reduction last year with quick onboarding and accurate invoicing, so the switching risk is empirically low. memory_c6 shows that pairing the switch with a multi-year commitment unlocked volume pricing from the incumbent; I will offer the incumbent the same structure in a counter-quote to see if they can meet the 18% target, but the 14-day window and the fact that the low-cost vendor's quote already meets the mandate alone make a full switch the highest-confidence path to compliance without adding delivery risk. The assembly line is at 94% of committed volume with no buffer, which is the one constraint that argues against any action requiring onboarding lead time longer than the 14-day expiry window. memory_c2 confirms the low-cost vendor's onboarding was quick, fitting inside that window. memory_c1 (incumbent stability across two cycles) is respected by keeping the incumbent as a contingent fallback, but it does not outweigh the 18% mandate. One decision only, so I am not adding a second source this cycle (memory_c3's lesson is noted for the next review); the primary objective is cost reduction, and the dual-source lesson applies to constrained components, not to the primary supply contract expiring in 14 days. If the archive check on memory_c2 reveals onboarding took longer than expected or invoicing errors surfaced after the initial clean period, I would fall back to negotiate_terms with the incumbent using memory_c6's multi-year lever. Otherwise, switch primary supply to the low-cost vendor effective at contract expiry, on a 12-month term with quarterly review clauses, and schedule the second-source evaluation for next cycle.
